# Maria's Story

Maria sits in the studio at 2 a.m., the blue glow of her monitor the only light in the darkened office. She's been here for six hours straight, refining the subtle movements of a character's hand—a gesture meant to convey vulnerability. Her colleagues have long since gone home, but Maria finds the silence comforting. The empty building feels safer than most places.

She's twenty-one now, a junior animator at a mid-sized studio in the city, and by most measures, she's doing well. Her technical skills are strong; her director praised her work on the last project. But Maria knows the real reason she stays late. It's harder to think when she's focused on the pixel-perfect arc of a finger, the microsecond timing of a blink. When she's working, she can keep her mind tethered to something manageable.

The memories don't stay buried for long, though. They surface without warning—usually in the evening, when the day's momentum fades and her brain finally quiets down. Maria will be sitting in her apartment, and suddenly she's twelve years old again, standing in the hallway of her childhood home, listening to her parents fight. Not just arguing. Fighting. Her father's voice rising into something unrecognizable, her mother's sharp responses, the sound of something breaking. She remembers the specific shade of the hallway carpet, the way her hands shook as she pressed herself against the wall, trying to be invisible.

What bothers Maria most isn't the memory itself—it's that her body doesn't know the difference between then and now. Her heart rate spikes the same way. Her breathing becomes shallow. Last week, a coworker raised his voice during a meeting, and Maria felt her vision narrow, felt the familiar surge of panic that made her want to bolt from the conference room. She didn't, of course. She sat perfectly still and waited for it to pass, a skill she's perfected over years of practice.

The hypervigilance is exhausting. Maria notices everything now—the way people's jaws tighten when they're irritated, the subtle shift in tone that precedes anger. She watches for these signs constantly, as if she can prevent something bad from happening if she just stays alert enough. In relationships, this has been catastrophic. She's had two brief romantic connections since high school, both ending when her partners couldn't understand why she flinched when they raised their voice, or why she needed so much reassurance that they weren't angry with her.

She doesn't sleep well. Most nights, she lies awake for hours, her mind cycling through worst-case scenarios—not just about her own safety, but about whether she's doomed to recreate her parents' relationship. Whether she'll become her mother, or somehow attract her father's rage. These thoughts feel as real as the walls around her, as inevitable as gravity.

Her parents separated when she was fourteen, and the violence stopped. Maria threw herself into art as a way to process what she'd witnessed, to create worlds where she had control. Animation became her refuge—she could rewrite scenes, undo moments, make characters behave exactly as she wanted them to. In the digital space, there were no surprises, no sudden explosions of anger.

But lately, even animation feels less protective. The hypervigilance follows her into her work. She second-guesses her creative choices, wondering if they're too dark, if they reveal something broken inside her. She's started turning down social invitations, finding excuses to stay home or work late. The isolation doesn't bother her the way it probably should.

Maria knows something is wrong. She just doesn't know how to fix it yet.
